content.thinking:
I'm starting to draft the structure, checking whether the lathe function supports a scale parameter for building the stone shape, and realizing it doesn't -- so I'll need to use scaled sphere geometry instead to get the non-uniform shape I want.

I'm designing a custom rock geometry helper: starting from an icosahedron, jittering vertex radii with noise for a faceted boulder look, and clamping the top vertices to create a flattened plateau surface for the top stone.

Since each rock needs independent per-vertex jitter without merge artifacts, I'll generate them separately rather than merging geometries, then apply a surface paint function using moss coverage based on surface normal and noise.

Adding crack and mottle logic...

Working out the stacked rock dimensions: a base boulder and a balanced egg-shaped stone on top, solving for center heights so the plateau lands at the target top height around 0.33.

The upper stone's bottom sinks slightly into the lower boulder, which is fine since it's hidden inside. I'm figuring out the lower boulder's flat-bottom clamp so it doesn't sink too far below the floor, staying within about 2% of total height.

I'm planning the top of the stone pile — flat plateau faces, moss pillows, hanging moss tufts, and small flowers draped around the rim. For ground clutter I'm adding pebbles, fern cards, mushrooms with lathe-shaped caps and stems, a ring of grass cards, and small flowers, plus a glowing sigil decal on the front face of the lower boulder visible from the hero camera angle, along with a few glowing mushroom caps for extra ambiance.

Now I'm sketching the texture SVGs: a grey fur tuft shape (teardrop with fur strand lines, tintable by part color) and a coloured grass blade tuft with multiple blades in two shades of green plus lighter tips, meant to be used directly as cards.

Continuing on, I'm planning the remaining decal textures—moss fringe drips, a central-rib fern leaf, a gold-capped tassel with green silk strands, and a dendro sigil disc: a gold filigree ring surrounding a dark teal field with a glowing bright green leaf-and-rays motif so the glow shows through while the dark areas stay transparent against the stone.

Then I move to the medallion filigree plane, a gold scroll ring with darker orange shading lines reserved for a gem socket, and start working out the collar ribbon pattern—teal fabric with gold stitch dashes placed using torus UV coordinates, computing a diamond motif along the ring direction so gold diamonds repeat evenly around the neckline.

For the eyes, I'm settling on amber-gold or leafy green-gold tones to contrast with the rust panda fur—going with iris colors in bright green-yellow with a pale highlight and darker forest shade, plus a warm tinted blush for the cheeks, before moving on to the cheek ruff shape.

For the tufted texture, I'm planning to use scattered cards rather than extruded fur spikes, coloring them via the same paint function used for the head so cheeks stay white and the rest rust-toned. I'm roughing out counts: around 40 cheek tufts, 50 along the body edges, 70 for the tail, and 20 on the chest, each small in scale—accepting that cards will look flatter than the celshaded surfaces but good enough for this pass.

Now I'm working out the head's bone and part placement in world space: the skull sphere, cheek puffs, snout, and nose, each positioned relative to the head joint with specific offsets and scales so the muzzle, cheeks, and nose highlight read correctly.

I'm figuring out the mouth and jaw geometry—skipping the thin lip-line curves in favor of modeling the jaw as a hinge joint that rotates slightly open, with a cream-colored lower jaw sphere positioned and scaled to sit just below and forward of the upper skull.

I'm adding the interior mouth detail: a dark maroon ellipsoid for depth, a small pink tongue on the jaw bone, and tiny white fang spikes near the mouth corners pointing downward. Then I move on to whiskers, sweeping thin cream-colored strands fanning outward from each side of the muzzle, tuning the radius and sides so they read as fine and delicate rather than chunky.

Now I'm skipping the forehead stripe idea in favor of a gold ear clip accent, and working out the precise eye placement using spherical coordinates on the head - calculating the azimuth, elevation, and resulting x/y/z offsets so the eye decals and eyebrow dots land symmetrically on the face.

For the tear marks running from eyes to muzzle, I'm defining them as thin line segments in 3D space and painting any surface point that falls within a small distance threshold of that segment, which should work as long as the line stays close enough to the skull and snout geometry.

Now I'm defining the fur patterns and body coloring -- using a mottled rust pattern for the back fading into darker fur on the belly, considering whether to add thin ink outlines along the fur edges but leaning toward skipping heavy outlines to match a softer, Genshin-style look, with darker fur starting on the legs and lower flanks like a real red panda.

Working out the leg and paw shading using position-based fur masking, keeping paws near-black while rust color stays on the upper thighs connecting to the body, and now sketching the logic for tail ring bands with a zigzag offset for the stripe pattern.

Thinking through the ring palette, alternating a bright rust-orange and deep rust-red with a dark chestnut tip and a plain base band, plus a gold clasp accent near the top of the tail, and figuring out how to sample the color along the tail's path using its closest-point parameter.

Now I'm working out the shading logic — cards get flat lit/shadow coloring based on their normal against the light, planning to skip teeth detail but keep the fangs, and thinking through how to place eye decals on the skull surface. For foot placement, I'm computing ground height by raycasting downward onto the stone plateau since it's flat, and working out shoulder joint positions for the front legs relative to the body's coordinate frame.

For the front limbs, I'm checking that the shoulder-to-wrist distance is short relative to total leg segment length, which means the elbow needs to fold back a bit to look natural rather than splaying out — adjusting segment lengths and shoulder height so the pose reads as a nearly vertical red panda leg with a slight bend.

Now for the hind legs, I'm placing the hip root and working out thigh and shin lengths so the heel sits behind and the toe forward, checking if the hip-to-heel distance fits within the thigh+shin reach — it's short enough that the knee folds forward into a semi-crouch, matching a real red panda's bent hind posture. I'm also recalculating the belly's bottom y-coordinate from the body root position.

Still working out tube cross-sections...

Now I'm setting up the toe chains - three small capsule segments branching off each foot tip, parented to the foot joint with tapered radii, and adding claw spikes at the tips.

Writing SVG texture strings...

Still writing SVG paths...

For the moss hangers, I'm thinking through orientation — drawn with the tip at top and wide base at bottom, but since they hang and are viewed from downstream, the root attachment edge actually appears upside-down at the top of the card.

Now I'm sketching the fern asset: a tall viewBox with a central stem and procedurally generated leaflet pairs rising and rotating along it, filled in layered greens.

Next I'm designing the tassel icon — a hanging knot with a gold bead and neck ring at the root end, and teal-green strands fanning out toward the tip — before moving on to sketch out the sigil decal.

For the sigil, I'm planning a double gold ring with a dark teal inner disc and a glowing green leaf rune at the center, making sure stroke widths scale properly for the raster size. Then I move to the medal's filigree texture, sketching a gold petal ring made of rotated ellipses around the center.

For the gem-bearing plane, I decide the petal ring stays flat with an empty cut-out hole at the center so the gem shows through from behind. I also sketch a small flower texture with a green stem, white petals, and a yellow center for use on cards.

Now I move to the mushroom: I lathe a cap profile defining the curved outline from the stem axis outward to the cap edge, and consider a glowing teal variant for a bioluminescent version.

Each cap stays a single flat color with tiny cream sphere spots added on top, paired with a cream capsule stem. I scatter small rock-helper pebbles nearby using stone paint, and add floating glowing octahedra motes plus extruded leaf shapes swirling around the panda in green tones with soft glow, placing several leaves and diamond motes at varied positions. I'm also starting to plan out the joint hierarchy for the panda's skeleton.

Working through the ear joints, leg and toe counts, and the total joint tally, then setting up hinge-role ear bones at the ear base. For moss hanging on the stone rim, I'm figuring out how to scatter upward-facing frames along the rim slope using surface normal filters so the moss cards hang naturally from the stone's upper edge.

Since the frames built from a hit point have no bone by default, I need to explicitly bind all the stone clutter -- moss cards, rock paint decals -- to a single fixed joint like the base, rather than letting them auto-bind to the nearest joint which could be a paw or leg joint and cause them to move unnaturally when the figure is posed.

For body tufts I'll scatter cards across the body sweep surface, inheriting bone weights from the hit so they deform properly with the mesh. For the ears, I'm positioning the joint and extrusion base slightly inward and sunken, then handling paint/rim coloring by checking the face normal's z-component to distinguish front, back, and rim surfaces after extrusion.

Working out the inner ear shape as a zigzag ellipse outline, confirming the symmetry logic holds when mirrored for the other side. Then I move to the collar: it's a torus placed along the neck path's tangent direction near the top, sized slightly larger than the neck radius there, with the head's cheek fur draping down to partially cover its front.

I check whether the collar sits behind or in front of the skull's back edge and conclude it falls just behind the head, so it'll peek out from the sides like a ribbon. Then I plan the medallion hanging from the chest -- placing it by casting a ray onto the front chest surface to find the right hit point, offsetting slightly along the normal so it rests naturally, and adding two cord sweeps running up from the collar to the medallion.

Now I'm sketching the cord path draped over the body and neck surfaces, V-shaped from collar to medal and mirrored on the other side, with a thin gold sweep for the cord itself. I note the skeleton joints are fine as-is, then start thinking through actually writing the full code, including scattering small cheek tufts onto the cheek sphere parts using filtered hit normals.

Writing rock geometry function...

I'll use detail level 2 for larger stones and detail 1 for pebbles, with the deformation deterministic so shared vertices stay consistent, and clamp the top to form a flat plateau. Flat shading will give each face its own normal for a faceted rock look.

For moss, I'm thinking of small scaled spheres painted mossy green placed along the plateau rim, draping slightly over the edges near where the panda's paws rest. I'm calculating the plateau's actual width and depth from the rock's radius and height clamp so I can position the moss and paws correctly relative to each other.

Now I'm working out the upper stone's dimensions so its widest point sits just above the lower boulder, checking that the overlap region stays hidden inside the boulder's footprint so the two pieces blend seamlessly.

Solving for the bottom clamp so the boulder's world-bottom sits at -0.012, giving bot ≈ -0.64 and top at cy+ry=0.185. Now moving to cel shading defaults for the stone's shadow.

I also need moss placement on the lower boulder's rim where its top faces upward, then set up the paint functions: mottled green patterns for lit and shadowed moss, a mottled gray-blue stone pattern, and a base stone paint blending noise with the surface normal's y-component.

Still writing stone paint logic...

Still writing face paint function...

Still tuning the zigzag teeth geometry...

Adding more facial markings...

Shifting to a muted lilac feels right. For ears, I'll keep the back dark with a cream inner front. Thinking through the neck and chest colors—rust at the top transitioning to a dark rusty-black underside with a white chin—and the tail should cap with a dark brown tip.

Now I'm sketching out the API structure: card options covering bone, color, flow, size, lean, bend, and spin; decal options for positioning and rotation; and chain setup for the spine and digits, where a two-point path gives a single joint. For the tail, I'll use a six-segment chain with default naming, then sweep a ring shape along it with color, sides, caps, and smoothing options.

I'm checking joint alignment -- the chest sweep radius should reach the front z-coordinate where the neck overlaps, and the neck chain needs its two joints positioned so the head joint lands just inside the skull's z-span. I'm also planning cheek tufts and neck fluff for extra fur detail, confirming the stone base sits below the panda's paws, and assigning roles like "tail" and "leg" to the relevant chains before finalizing the joint and spine structure.

Now I'm figuring out roles for the remaining joints -- neck, head, jaw, and ear hinges -- and confirming the foot tip joint gets its digit role automatically. I'm also setting up the toe chain parent references, double-checking the limb bend count won't throw errors, then moving into writing the actual code: importing the glow helper and rng utility, defining a flat green gem glow, and placing ground clutter like flowers and boulders so nothing collides with the tail, finishing with a lathe profile for a low ground disc.

Checking the lathe outline closes correctly with lowest contact at y=0, then switching the ground to a low-poly decagon by adjusting segment count instead of scaling. I'm planning to scatter grass tufts and flowers across the ground surface using normal-based placement with a minimum distance, then write the whole file in one pass while verifying the top height constant against a ray check.
